extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations; public relations managers and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on organizational public responsibility, the role of public relations in reporting/internalizing responsibility, and standards for social reports/audits; also discussion of professionalism in public relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public responsibility (Preston & Post)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations should take responsibility for primary and secondary involvements — i.e., produce quality products and services and make a profit (primary) and clean up the fallout from those activities (secondary) such as pollution, product hazards, or employment discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'public responsibility' as the operative criterion because it limits responsibility to consequences of the organization's own primary and secondary activities rather than an unbounded set of social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social responsibility (distinct concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'social responsibility' includes broader, third-category issues (general social problems) and 'has no boundary' — the organization can never define where its responsibilities begin and end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'social responsibility' as a broader, less practical standard for organizational action; prefer 'public responsibility' when setting actionable PR scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a public relations problem
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization faces a public relations problem when it has consequences on publics or when publics have consequences upon the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame public responsibility work as addressing these reciprocal consequences through communication and management action.

rubrics_metrics.name: PR's communicative role in organizational responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations is a communication function: PR managers seldom have the power to make organizations publicly responsible but can (a) communicate to organizational subsystems what publics believe to be irresponsible behaviors and (b) report to publics what the organization has done or is doing to rectify irresponsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus PR efforts on accurate internal reporting of public perceptions and transparent external reporting of remedial actions; accept that PR influences decisions by informing other decision-makers rather than unilaterally implementing change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal reporting / involvement in decision making
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations personnel should communicate public perceptions to top management and organizational subsystems and be 'inside the door' when management decisions are made rather than waiting to announce decisions afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PR managers should seek participation in top-management decision processes, ask policy-relevant questions (e.g., about personnel policies, vulnerability to interest-group attacks, positions on government policy), and not simply expect their advice to be followed at all times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issues management process (Jones & Chase)
rubrics_metrics.description: Issues management involves four stages: 1) Issue identification; 2) Issue analysis; 3) Issue change strategy options; 4) Issue action programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the four-stage framework as an internal process to alert management early to issues of public concern and to include those issues in decision making to prevent costly external actions (e.g., regulation, litigation, board contests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employee communication's expanded role
rubrics_metrics.description: Employee communication must do more than inform employees about management policy; it must sensitize employees to public responsibility so that all members of the organization practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design internal communications to build employee understanding of the organization's public consequences and responsibilities, not merely to transmit directives.

rubrics_metrics.name: External reporting: social reports and social audits
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations usually report their public responsibility through social reports or, theoretically, social audits that quantify social 'goods' and 'bads' and balance them similarly to financial audits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer social reports in practice due to the high cost and measurement difficulty of comprehensive social audits; when possible, aim for external validation and rigorous standards analogous to financial audits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal social audit standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal social audit would be constructed by an outside accounting firm and would meet the same standards as a financial audit, quantifying public responsibility and balancing dollar values of social benefits and harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge limits: few organizations produce quantified social audits because costs and valuation difficulties often outweigh perceived benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents and examples of social reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Social reports should document topics such as regulatory issues, safety, equal employment opportunity, programs for minorities and women, plant closings/relocations, philanthropic activities, environmental and energy efforts, and tax and economic impacts (illustrated by General Motors' Public Interest Report and the Clearinghouse on Corporate Social Responsibility reporting form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comprehensive topic lists and standardized reporting forms to make social reports informative and comparable across organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of good social reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Good social reporting is characterized by consistency, objectivity, comparability, and relevance to appropriate social concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-serving reports: report consistently year-to-year, include candid discussion of shortcomings and adverse social impacts, and provide material relevant to stakeholders; aim for comparability across time and peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candid disclosure of shortcomings
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective social reports candidly discuss problems and what the organization has done about them (e.g., Eastern Gas & Fuel's acknowledgment of rising accident rates; ARCO's candid discussion of difficulty finding women/minorities in professional areas and linking executive pay to EEO performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include frank assessments of negative performance and specific corrective measures; candidness increases credibility and distinguishes high-quality social reporting from token statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of public responsibility to nonbusiness organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: All organizations (not just businesses) have primary and secondary involvements and should monitor and communicate their consequences on publics (examples: EPA, hospitals, churches, NRA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend social reporting and internal issue monitoring to nonbusiness organizations where primary activities produce secondary economic/social consequences; tailor reports to the organization's mission and stakeholder concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of PR staff as 'communication technicians'
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners trained only as 'communication technicians' often lack the technical knowledge and skills to participate effectively in decision processes at the level of corporate policy; sophistication beyond communication skills is needed for the expanded PR role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in professional development that builds technical knowledge, policy understanding, and strategic decision-making abilities so PR staff can contribute meaningfully to organizational responsibility decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism criteria for public relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations as a profession should have an identifiable body of knowledge and an enforceable code of ethics; professions are also characterized by values, associations, norms, body of knowledge, and education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and adhere to professional standards, codes of ethics, formal education/training, and professional associations to raise practice standards and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits and organizational impact of professionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionals bring outside contacts, autonomy, and an ethic that can force organizations to innovate and be more responsible; practitioners practicing two-way symmetric PR attempt to change both the organization and its publics and typically require professional ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage hiring or cultivating professionals (internally or as consultants) to support two-way symmetric approaches and to provide early-warning and corrective perspectives; recognize organizational resistance in rigid or formalized firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and constraints of consultants/agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultants and agency professionals can provide fresh outlooks and innovation, but agencies may be pressured by client demand to provide press agentry or two-way asymmetric services, which can strain professionals aiming for ethical/professional practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using or working in agencies, anticipate commercial pressures and build safeguards (client selection, internal ethics, scope agreements) that allow professionals to maintain standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation management for PR influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations managers should not expect their advice to be followed at all times; the important objective is communicating public perceptions to decision-makers so those perceptions can be considered in management decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure PR success partly by whether public concerns are communicated into the decision process (e.g., issues are identified and considered), not solely by immediate adoption of PR recommendations.
